zones.label: Column 1

Used only as a secondary identification aid, not as a diplomatic transcription. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Ikanimo is the emphatic adverb glossed simply as 'very' or 'much'; the entry is not an interrogative despite the following related forms.

runs.text: Adu. De q̃ maneira, ou como.

lines.note: Ikanito shite asks in what manner or how. The Portuguese q̃ is an abbreviation in the print and is retained rather than expanded to que.
Ikanishitemo is glossed as 'in whatever manner it may be'; the next example tests the construction with a negative predicate.
Ikanishitemo naranu means that something cannot be done by any means. The Portuguese negative formulation continues into pode ser on the following row.
Pode ser completes 'by no means can it be'; this is the short Portuguese continuation of the preceding negative example, not an independent entry.
Ikake is firing at something with an arrow or firearm. The scan has c in Icaqe, not OCR e, and a line-end hyphen dividing eſpingar-da; the historical frecha is retained.
Da completes eſpingarda, the firearm paired with an arrow in the preceding row. The ampersand and c continue the printed 'etc.' formula.
This second ikake entry concerns repairing a metal vessel by casting or soldering, not shooting. The final va- belongs to vaſo on the next row.

runs.text: ſo de metal quebrado fundindo aquella parte

lines.note: The broken metal vessel is repaired by melting or casting the missing part; the relative clause continues into que falta below. No modern technical term is substituted.
Que falta specifies the part that is missing and completes the repair definition; its brevity does not change its status as a physical body row.

Ikarakashi, ikarakasu, ikarakaita describes stiffening or setting a body part forcefully. The initial is an upright capital I; aita is retained as the historical principal part rather than modernized.

runs.text: corpo com brio, ou ira. Vt,

lines.note: The gloss specifies pride or anger, and kata wo ikarakasu begins the example of squaring or stiffening the shoulders. The divided icara- continues in the next row.

runs.text: Enteſar os hombros. i, Moſtrarſe ſo-

lines.note: Caſu completes ikarakasu. The Portuguese explains both stiffening the shoulders and displaying pride; the final ſo- continues as ſoberbo.
Berbo completes ſoberbo. Hiji wo ikarakasu gives the elbow counterpart and Idẽ refers back to the same meaning; Me- begins the following eye example.
Me- plus uo gives the eye as object in me wo ikarakasu. Regalar os olhos here means opening or staring with the eyes, not giving a gift.
Ikari is an anchor. Ikari wo utsu and the divided alternative vorosu introduce dropping or lowering the anchor; the l is the alternative marker, not part of the Japanese.
Roſu completes vorosu, lowering the anchor. The new example ikari wo vokosu, alternatively toru, concerns weighing it rather than dropping it.
Toru completes the alternative verb in the anchor example; leuar ancora means weighing or lifting the anchor, retaining the historical u/v spelling.
Ikari, ikaru, ikatta is becoming angry. Agastarſe supplies that meaning; the r is not added to the abbreviated u principal part in the canonical text.
This ikari is anger, distinct from the preceding anchor noun. The example introduces restraining or soothing anger, with na- continued as nadamuru below.
Nadamuru and shizumuru complete the alternatives for calming anger. The Portuguese apla continues into aplacar without a securely printed terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.
Car completes aplacar a ira. Ikari wo vokosu then illustrates arousing anger or becoming angry, as the repeated Agaſtarſe confirms.
Ikarikuji is the anchorage term in this cluster; the initial capital I beside the rule was omitted by OCR. The scan's Ancoragem is kept without selecting a narrower modern nautical sense.
Ikarigoe is an angry voice. The worn headword is read Icarigoye from its surviving initial and medial strokes together with the explicit anger gloss, not OCR Acaigoye; the medial r is faint.
Ikarimanako denotes angry eyes, directly matched by olhos irados. It is a separate compound headword, not a continuation of the voice example.
Ikarizura is an angry face or expression. The scan supports a capital I and the doubled zz; the Portuguese retains its printed historical forms rather than being modernized.
Ikaruga is described only as a small bird of that name. The capital I and the damaged letters of Paßarinho are recovered from the scan and bird context; no species identification is inserted.
Ikasama is labelled an adverb and glossed poruentura, 'perhaps' or 'perchance'. This historical sense should not be replaced by the modern cheating sense.
Ikasamanimo receives the same adverbial meaning through Idem. The longer form is a genuine separate entry, with the repeated adverb label.
Ikata is a mould for cast objects, with projectiles and devotional images among the examples in the Portuguese list. The printed pilouros and veronicas remain unchanged.
Ikatei is glossed 'in whatever manner'. It leads into the attributive form ikateino on the next row rather than forming one headword with it.
Ikateino means 'whatever' or 'any'; ikateino koto begins the example that is completed by naritomo below.
Naritomo completes ikateino koto naritomo, 'whatever the thing may be'. The scan supports the unusual printed Quelquer, which is preserved rather than normalized to Qualquer.
Ikaeshi is shooting back or returning fire. The scan supports eita, not OCR cita, as the abbreviated past form; the definition continues with the projectile or weapon below.
The response is made with an arrow or firearm shot. Frecha and eſpingarda retain the source's historical spellings and complete the verb definition.
Ikayoona is the adjectival 'whatever' or 'of whatever kind'. The visible caron distinguishes this printed long-o notation from a circumflex.

runs.text: Adu. Em que maneira, ou em

lines.note: Ikayooni is an adverb meaning 'in what manner' or 'in whatever manner'. The right edge shows em without a terminal hyphen; the preposition continues syntactically, not as a divided word.
Qualquer maneira completes the second paraphrase of ikayooni. The scan's e in maneira corrects OCR mancira, without changing the word's historical spelling.
Ikayoonimo is glossed 'in whatever manner'; the concessive or indefinite force is completed by que seja on the next physical row.
Que ſeja completes 'whatever manner it may be'. It belongs to the preceding adverbial entry and is not a separately translated Japanese fragment.
Ikayooni naritomo is assigned the same adverbial sense by Idem. The phrase remains spaced as printed rather than joined to match neighbouring forms.
Ikayoono is attributive 'whatever'. The example begins ikayoono fi- and continues with ma, making fima the Japanese word for time or opportunity here.
The example concludes fima irutomo, followed by the upright citation label Mon. The Portuguese says 'whatever occupation'; the printed Qualquer is one word, and oc- continues below.

Cupação completes occupação, and que tenhais addresses the reader's occupation or business. The translation remains literal to the dictionary even where it is not a word-for-word rendering of the Japanese.
Ikazuchi is thunder or a thunderbolt, as trouão and coriſco indicate. The doubled zz is part of the Jesuit spelling and is not simplified.

runs.text: Algũs vocabulos ſe deixarão aqui que parecem de

lines.note: An editorial explanation begins: some words resembling counting expressions are left here. The scan has ſe rather than OCR ſo; this is body text, not a running header.

runs.text: contas, mas não o ſão, por que ſe não vſão cõ-

lines.note: The explanation says these are not ordinary counting forms and are not commonly used beyond the listed expressions. The thin medial long s gives vſão, not OCR vão; cõ- continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: munmente mais que da maneira que aqui ſe eſ-

lines.note: Munmente completes cõmunmente across the column break. The editorial note limits these words to the ways in which they are written here; eſ- continues into eſcreuem.

runs.text: creuem, ſem ſe multiplicar como as de mais cõ

lines.note: The forms are not multiplied or varied like other counting expressions. The scan supplies the t missing from OCR multiplicar; cõ continues into contas without an added hyphen.

runs.text: tas que deixamos pera ſeu lugar.

lines.note: Tas completes contas, which the editors reserve for their proper place. This concludes the introductory explanation before the separate lexical entry Icca.
Ikka is one house or household, paraphrased hitotsu no ie. The scan has two c letters and a nasal abbreviation in Hũa; neither is supplied merely from the modern word.

runs.text: Os parentes, ou os da meſ-

lines.note: Goikka no shu denotes members or relatives of a great lord's household. The Portuguese begins 'the relatives, or those of the same', continuing below.
Ma completes meſma, and the phrase identifies the household or family of a great lord. This contextualizes the preceding honorific goikka example.
Ikkaku is 'one horn', paraphrased hitotsu no tsuno. The following maxim develops the one-horn comparison rather than adding another dictionary definition.
Shukaku ooshi to iedomo begins the concessive comparison of many horns with one. The example's iccacuni has a lowercase initial in the scan, unlike OCR Iccacuni.

runs.text: Ainda que haja animais de mui-

lines.note: Shikazu completes 'does not equal'. The Portuguese says that although there are animals with many horns; its verb is haja, not OCR baja, and mui- continues below.

runs.text: tos cornos como veado, &c. todauia não che-

lines.note: Tos completes muitos, with deer as the example. The argument contrasts such animals with the one-horned animal; che- is divided from the following gão.

runs.text: gão ao vnicorne, ou a bada que tem hum ſoo cor

lines.note: The animals do not equal the unicorn or bada, described as having a single horn. Cor continues into corno with no secure printed terminal hyphen, which is therefore not invented.

runs.text: no. Comparaſe tambem a hum homem valen-

lines.note: No completes corno. The gloss then applies the comparison to one brave person; valen- is divided at the end of this row.

runs.text: te em comparação doutros muitos menos valen

lines.note: The one brave person is contrasted with many less brave people. The final valen continues below, but unlike the preceding row its right edge does not establish a hyphen.
Tes completes valentes, and the printed &c. closes the comparison. S marks written usage, not a further Japanese word.
This separate ikkaku means a guest from elsewhere, not a horn. The scan supports doubled cc and hoſpede rather than OCR boſpede; S again marks a written-language use.
Ikkai is one prohibition or precept, paraphrased hitotsu no imashime. Two c letters are visible; pro continues into prohibição without a supplied line-end hyphen.
Hibição completes prohibição, the second Portuguese gloss for the one-precept entry. The short row is retained independently.
Ikkan is a brushstroke or a letter, paraphrased hitofude. The two c letters are visible; the Portuguese moves from a stroke of the pen to a written letter.
This ikkan is one pole, hitotsu no sao. The Portuguese first gives a fishing rod, with a second kind of pole continuing below.
The alternative is a pole belonging to a vessel. The worn middle of embarcação caused OCR embaz ação; the visible sequence and nautical context support the contiguous word. S marks written usage.

runs.text: Hũa viſta, ou paſſada que ſe dà a algũ

lines.note: Another ikkan means a look or perusal of a book. The final algũ is singular and has no visible following s; it modifies liuro on the next line.
Liuro completes the object of the glance or perusal, and S labels the usage as written. The word retains the printed u rather than modern livro.

runs.text: Hum frio. i, Hum inuerno. Vt,

lines.note: Ikkan is one cold season, hence a winter. The Japanese example starts Ic- and continues into iccan wo shinogu or tooru below.
Canuo completes iccanuo; shinogu and tooru express getting through a winter. The Portuguese Paßar hum begins the same translation.
Inuerno completes 'to pass a winter'. This is the final continuation of that ikkan entry, before the gilding term.

runs.text: Certo modo de dourado com ouro moi-

lines.note: Ikkake is a gilding technique using ground gold. The moido word is physically divided moi-do; no chemical or craft process beyond the printed explanation is supplied.
Do completes moido, followed by gold reduced to a pulp or paste. The printed desfeito is retained, rather than changing its s allograph from contextual expectations.
Ikkakeji receives the same meaning as the preceding gilding term through Idem. The gi belongs to the headword and is not a Portuguese abbreviation.
Itchi means union or agreement, and itchi suru means becoming united. Both occurrences have cc in the scan; OCR Ichi and Iechi each lose or misread one consonant.
Hum corpo por amizade, & vnião completes the idea of becoming one body through friendship and union. It is the translation of the preceding Japanese verb phrase.
Itchoo counts one bird, paraphrased hitotsu no tori. The circumflex on the headword is retained as printed, rather than inferred from the following homophone.
The next itchoo is one morning, hito asa. The Portuguese menhãa is a historical printed form and is not modernized to manhã.
Ikko is one torch, hitotsu no taimatsu. The scan has doubled cc; the Portuguese definition continues with materials used to make the torch.

runs.text: ſe faz em Iapão de achas de pinheiro, ou de bã

lines.note: The torch is made in Japan from pieces of pine or bamboo. The bã is the first portion of the bamboo word continued below, with its printed nasal abbreviation retained.

runs.text: bus ſecos, ou de palha, &c. S.

lines.note: Bus completes the bamboo word, followed by dry material or straw. S labels written usage; this closes the torch entry, not the subsequent 'one person' example.
Ikko here is a single person or attendant. Komono ikko no tei- starts an example of appearing with just one servant; tei is divided from gia on the next row.

runs.text: Vai com hum ſoo moço a companhado.

lines.note: Gia completes the Japanese predication. The Portuguese describes going accompanied by only one servant; its visible a companhado spacing is retained rather than normalized to acompanhado.
Ikkoo, paraphrased hitomuki, has an emphatic 'in any case' sense. The headword begins with capital I and the example has two c letters; both carons are retained from the scan.
Ni tanomi zonzuru completes the emphatic request. The Portuguese peço vos reiterates asking earnestly or by every means, with ca- continued below.

runs.text: ſo, ou por todas as vias. ¶

lines.note: So completes caſo, followed by 'by every means'. The negative example ikkoo naranu is then introduced and translated in the next row.
The negative example means that something cannot be done under any circumstances. This short Portuguese line finishes the emphatic adverb entry.

runs.text: Hum eſpaço de tempo como infinito.

lines.note: This ikkoo denotes a period of time described as almost infinite. The damaged middle of eſpaço contains p rather than OCR t; the headword's circumflex differs from the preceding adverb's caron.
Ikkoo is one mouth, hitotsu no kuchi. Doubled cc and the u in Fitotçuno are recovered from the scan; the roman Ic- starts a divided Japanese example, not italic punctuation.

runs.text: Falar de duas maneiras por hũa

lines.note: Ic- plus cô gives ikkoo, followed by ryoozetsu: speaking in two incompatible ways from one mouth. The visible mark on riôjet is a circumflex; the Portuguese continues into meſma boca.
Meſma boca completes the one-mouth explanation of double speech. This belongs to the preceding example rather than introducing a new anatomical term.

Ikkoboshi means overturning or pouring out completely. The scan supplies oita, Entornar and the contiguous derramar, correcting missing letters and a false OCR space without modernizing the inflection.
The gloss describes pouring out as by overturning. Ame ic- begins the rain example continued on f259; the printed em borcando spacing is kept and the catchword is not appended to this body line.

zones.label: Isolated bottom mark
zones.note: The isolated italic S. is visible to the left of the catchword. Its precise function is uncertain; it is preserved separately without asserting that it is a gathering signature or attaching it conjecturally to the prose above.

lines.note: The isolated italic S. is retained from the bottom margin. Its function is uncertain; it is not assigned conjecturally to a gathering signature or to the preceding body entry.
